newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan court deals blow to Yasukuni war shrine.
newsitem.headline: Japan court deals blow to Yasukuni war shrine.

text.p: In a landmark decision on the separation of state and religion, Japan's Supreme Court ruled on Wednesday that taxpayers' money could not be used for offerings at a controversial war shrine.
The court said local government cash offerings to Tokyo's Yasukuni Shrine, dedicated to Japan's 2.6 million war dead from World War Two and previous conflicts, were unconstitutional.
It ordered local authorities in Ehime Prefecture, 720 km (450 miles) southwest of Tokyo, to pay back to the prefecture 166,000 yen ($1,360) in offerings they made at the shrine from 1981 to 1986.
It is the first time the Supreme Court has ruled as unconstitutional public expenditure at Yasukuni Shrine, where war dead are symbolically enshrined as Shinto deities.
Dating from the 19th century, they include several Class-A war criminals such as General Hideki Tojo, Japan's prime minister in World War Two.
In its decision, the court said the offerings were a religious act and therefore violated Article 20 of the constitution.
Article 20, which guarantees freedom of religion, says no religious organisation may receive any privileges from the state and the state should refrain from religious activity.

Shinto, Japan's ancient animistic religion, was the state religion until 1945, with the emperor as its spiritual head. Visitors to a Shinto shrine by tradition give cash gifts as forms of tribute to the enshrined gods.

Between 1981 and 1986, Ehime Prefecture sent a total of 166,000 yen ($1,360) in cash offerings to Yasukuni as well as to local Shinto shrines dedicated to the war dead as part of annual rites to comfort the spirits of the deceased.
In 1982, 24 Ehime residents complained that the offerings violated the constitution and filed a suit demanding that the cash be repaid to public coffers.
A local court in Ehime in 1989 first ruled in favour of returning the money.

But three years later, the Takamatsu High Court overturned the decision, saying prefectural authorities could make the offerings because the donations were within customary social practice and not based on deep religious faith.
Until Wednesday's decision, church-state issues had mainly been based on a 1977 Supreme Court ruling which said it was impossible to clearly separate state and religion.

In the 1977 ruling, the Supreme Court said a Shinto ceremony performed for the building of a public gymnasium did not in effect support a particular religion, and actions by the state should be judged on whether the purpose behind the action was of a religious nature or one widely accepted by custom.

Yasukuni Shrine has been the focus of other controversies. Last July, Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto, breaking a decade-long taboo on visits by prime ministers to the shrine, made a "private" visit on his birthday.
Following bitter criticism from China, South Korea and other Asian nations, Hashimoto has said he will not again visit the shrine while he is in office. ($1=122 yen)
